title: Chapter 5. Of Reason, and Science
paragraphs: When a man reasons, he does nothing else but conceive a total sum from the addition of parcels, or conceive a remainder from the subtraction of one sum from another. When this is done with words, it amounts to conceiving the consequence of the names of all the parts as taking us to the name of the whole — or, from the names of the whole and one part, taking us to the name of the other part. And though in some matters (as with numbers) men name other operations besides adding and subtracting — multiplying and dividing — these are really the same: multiplication is only the addition of equal things together, and division is only the subtraction of one thing as often as we can. These operations apply not only to numbers but to all kinds of things that can be added together or taken one from another. As arithmeticians teach addition and subtraction in numbers, so geometers teach the same in lines, figures (solid and superficial), angles, proportions, times, degrees of speed, force, power, and the like; logicians teach the same in consequences of words — adding two names together to make an affirmation, two affirmations to make a syllogism, many syllogisms to make a demonstration, and from the sum (or conclusion) of a syllogism subtracting one proposition to find the other. Writers on politics add together compacts to find men's duties; lawyers add together laws and facts to find what is right and wrong in private actions. In short, wherever there is room for addition and subtraction, there is room for reason; and where these have no place, reason has nothing at all to do.

From all this we can define — that is, determine — what is meant by the word reason when we count it among the faculties of the mind. Reason, in this sense, is nothing but the reckoning (that is, the adding and subtracting) of the consequences of general names agreed on for marking and signifying our thoughts. I say marking when we reckon by ourselves, and signifying when we demonstrate or argue our reckonings to other men.

And just as in arithmetic unpractised men must, and even professional accountants may often, make mistakes and tally falsely, so in any other subject of reasoning the ablest, most attentive, and most practised men may deceive themselves and infer false conclusions. Not that reason itself is anything other than right reason — just as arithmetic is a certain and infallible art — but no one man's reason, nor the reason of any number of men, constitutes that certainty, any more than an account is well cast up just because a great many men have unanimously approved it. So when there is a controversy in an account, the parties must by their own consent set up, as right reason, the reason of some arbitrator or judge whose verdict they will both abide by — otherwise their controversy must either come to blows or remain undecided, for want of a right reason constituted by nature. The same holds in all debates whatsoever. When men who think themselves wiser than everyone else clamour and demand right reason for judge, yet ask only that matters be settled by no one's reason but their own, this is as intolerable in human society as it would be in a card game, after trumps have been turned, for a player to use as trump on every occasion whichever suit he most happens to hold. For that is just what they do who insist that each of their passions, as it gains sway in them, shall be taken for right reason — especially in their own quarrels. By the very claim they lay to right reason, they betray that they lack it.

The use and end of reason is not the finding of the sum, and the truth, of one or a few consequences remote from the first definitions and settled meanings of names, but to begin at those, and then proceed from one consequence to another. For there can be no certainty in the final conclusion without certainty in all the affirmations and negations on which it was grounded and inferred. When the head of a household, in going over the books, casts up the totals of all the bills of expense into one sum — without paying attention to how each bill is summed up by the persons who hand them in, or what he is paying for — he gains nothing more than if he had passed the whole account in bulk, trusting to the skill and honesty of every accountant under him. So too in reasoning about all other things: a man who picks up his conclusions on the authority of authors, and does not trace them back to the first items in every reckoning (which are the meanings of names settled by definitions) wastes his labour, and knows nothing — he only believes.

When a man reckons without the use of words — which can be done with particular things, as when, on seeing some object, we guess what was likely to have come before it or what is likely to follow from it — and what he thought likely to follow does not follow, or what he thought likely to have preceded did not precede, this is called ERROR, and even the most prudent men are subject to it. But when we reason in words of general meaning, and arrive at a general inference that is false, then though it is commonly called error, it is in fact an ABSURDITY, or senseless speech. For error is only a deception, a presumption that something is past or to come, where, even though it was not past or not to come, no impossibility could be discovered. But when we make a general assertion, then unless it is true, its very possibility cannot be conceived. And words by which we conceive nothing except the sound itself are the words we call absurd, insignificant, and nonsense. So if a man were to talk to me of a Round Quadrangle, or the Accidents Of Bread In Cheese, or Immaterial Substances, or of A Free Subject, A Free Will, or of anything as 'free' apart from being free from being hindered by opposition, I would not say that he was in error, but that his words were without meaning — that is to say, absurd.

I said earlier (in the second chapter) that man surpasses all other animals in this faculty: that when he conceives anything whatsoever, he is inclined to inquire into the consequences of it, and what effects he can produce with it. To that I now add a further degree of the same excellence: that he can use words to reduce the consequences he finds to general rules, called theorems or aphorisms; that is, he can reason, or reckon, not only in number but in all other things, where one thing can be added to or subtracted from another.

But this privilege is mitigated by another — the privilege of absurdity, to which no living creature is subject but man alone. And among men, those most subject to it are those who profess philosophy. For what Cicero somewhere says of them is true beyond doubt: there is nothing so absurd but that it may be found in the books of the philosophers. The reason is plain. Not one of them begins his reasoning from definitions, or from the explanation of the names he is about to use — a method that has been used only in geometry, whose conclusions have for that very reason been made indisputable.

The first cause of absurd conclusions I ascribe to lack of method: that they do not begin their reasoning from definitions, that is, from the settled meanings of their words — as if they could cast up an account without knowing the value of the numerals One, Two, and Three.

And since (as I noted in the previous chapter) all bodies enter into the account under various considerations, and since these considerations bear various names, various absurdities arise from the confused and ill-fitting way these names are connected in assertions. And so —

The second cause of absurd assertions I ascribe to assigning names of bodies to accidents, or of accidents to bodies — as when men say that Faith Is Infused, or Inspired, when nothing can be poured or breathed into anything but a body; or that Extension Is Body; or that Phantasms Are Spirits, and the like.

The third I ascribe to giving the names of the accidents of bodies outside us to the accidents of our own bodies — as when men say that The Colour Is In The Body, or The Sound Is In The Air, and the like.
The fourth, to giving the names of bodies to names or speeches — as when men say that There Are Things Universal, or that A Living Creature Is A Genus, or A General Thing, and so on.
The fifth, to giving the names of accidents to names and speeches — as when men say, The Nature Of A Thing Is In Its Definition, or A Man's Command Is His Will, and the like.

The sixth, to the use of metaphors, tropes, and other rhetorical figures in place of proper words. For though it is allowable to say in everyday speech (for example) The Road Goes, Or Leads, This Way Or That, or The Proverb Says This Or That — although roads cannot walk, and proverbs cannot speak — yet in reckoning and the search for truth such phrases are not to be admitted.

The seventh, to names that signify nothing but are picked up and learned by rote from the Schools — like Hypostatical, Transubstantiate, Consubstantiate, Eternal-now, and the rest of the cant of the Schoolmen.

For anyone who can avoid these things, it is not easy to fall into absurdity, unless it be through the length of an account, in which he may perhaps forget what went before. For by nature all men reason alike, and reason well, when their principles are good. For who is so stupid as both to err in geometry and to persist in it once another has shown him his mistake?

From this it appears that reason is not, like sense and memory, born in us, nor acquired only through experience (as prudence is); it is gained by industry — first in aptly imposing names, and second in arriving at a good and orderly method by which to proceed from the elements (which are names), to assertions made by the connection of one name to another, and then to syllogisms (which are the connections of one assertion to another), until we come to a knowledge of all the consequences of the names involved in the matter in hand. This is what men call SCIENCE. And whereas sense and memory are only knowledge of fact, which is past and irrevocable, science is knowledge of consequences, and of the dependence of one fact on another: by which, from what we can presently do, we know how to do something else when we choose, or the like another time. For when we see how a thing comes about — by what causes, and in what way — then whenever the like causes come within our power, we see how to make them produce the like effects.

Children, then, are not endowed with reason at all until they have attained the use of speech. They are called reasonable creatures only because of the apparent possibility that they will have the use of reason in time to come. And the greater part of grown men, though they have the use of reasoning a little way (for instance in counting to some degree), find it of little use in everyday life. In ordinary life they govern themselves, some better, some worse, according to differences of experience, quickness of memory, and inclinations to various ends — but above all according to good or bad fortune, and the errors of one another. As for science, or sure rules for their actions, they are so far from it that they do not know what it is. They have taken geometry for conjuring. And as for the other sciences, those who have not been taught their beginnings, and a little progress in them — enough to see how they are acquired and built up — are on this point like children who, having no notion of generation, are made to believe by the women that their brothers and sisters are not born but found in the garden.

And yet those who have no science are in a better and nobler condition, with their natural prudence, than men who, by faulty reasoning or by trusting those who reason wrongly, fall into false and absurd general rules. For ignorance of causes and of rules does not set men so far off their way as does reliance on false rules — taking for the causes of what they aspire to, things that are not the causes, but rather the causes of the opposite.

To conclude: the light of human minds is plain words, but only when they have first been snuffed clean and purged of ambiguity by exact definitions. Reason is the pace; the growth of science, the path; and the benefit of mankind, the end. By contrast, metaphors and senseless or ambiguous words are like ignes fatui — the will-o'-the-wisps — and to reason on them is to wander among innumerable absurdities, ending in quarrelling, sedition, or contempt.

As much experience is prudence, so much science is sapience. We commonly have a single word, wisdom, for both; yet the Latins always distinguished prudentia from sapientia, assigning the first to experience, the second to science. To bring out the difference more clearly: suppose one man is gifted with an excellent natural skill and dexterity in handling his weapons, and another, on top of that dexterity, has acquired a science of where he can strike or be struck by his opponent in every possible posture and guard. The ability of the first stands to the ability of the second as prudence stands to sapience — both useful, but the second infallible. But those who, trusting only in the authority of books, follow the blind blindly, are like the man who, trusting in the false rules of a master of fence, ventures rashly upon an adversary who either kills or shames him.

The signs of science are of two sorts: some certain and infallible, others uncertain. Certain, when he who claims the science of any matter can teach it — that is, plainly demonstrate its truth to another. Uncertain, when only some particular events bear out his claim, and on many occasions prove things to be as he says they must. The signs of prudence are all uncertain, because to observe by experience and remember every circumstance that might change the outcome is impossible. But in any matter where a man has no infallible science to proceed by, to give up his own natural judgement and be guided instead by general maxims read in authors — which are subject to many exceptions — is a sign of folly, and is generally scorned under the name of pedantry. Even those men who in councils of the commonwealth love to show off their reading in politics and history rarely behave that way in their domestic affairs, where their own interest is at stake; there they have prudence enough for their private matters. But in public they study the reputation of their own wit more than the success of another man's business.
